newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. power firms say investments depend on returns.
newsitem.headline: U.S. power firms say investments depend on returns.

text.p: The United States could help ease India's chronic power shortage with huge investments to renovate its ailing plants if suitable returns were assured, a visiting U.S. trade official said on Tuesday.
Raymond Vickery, assistant secretary of Commerce, told a news conference that some 46 Indian power projects had been identified as suitable for renovation and modernisation.
But Vickery, leading a delegation of officials from 11 U.S. power firms, said to attract capital for the renovation of the power plants India needed to make the returns on the investments attractive.
"The money is there but the question is how to put the projects in a form which is bankable and can provide a suitable rate of return," Vickery said.
Asked how much money the U.S. firms might invest Vickery said:"We are looking at billions...but that is pure estimate as opposed to scientific."
"If all of them are worked on then it would mean an additional 13,000 megawatts of power...at $1 million for every kilowatt that amounts of $13 billion," Vickery said.
India in 1991 launched a market-oriented economic reforms programme, dismantling tariff barriers and inviting private and foreign investment into its economy.

India says it needs investments worth $79 billion to ease acute power shortages. It could add only 14,799 megawatts in power generation capacity during the first four years of its Eighth Five-Year Plan (1992-97), which had envisaged an addition of 30,858 megawatts in the five years.
"This growth cannot come from new projects alone, it must include renovation and modernisation of existing plants," Vickery said.
With many power plants operating at only 50-60 percent of rated capacity, Indian power officials are turning to renovation and modernisation to solve power shortages.
